payload.title: Ideal bicycle chain-drive speed ratio

model.title: Ideal bicycle chain-drive speed ratio
model.description: Unqualified proposal for human review: bounded no-slip transmission with controllable tooth counts and pedaling cadence, plus calculated chain travel and rotation rates.
assumptions: Front tooth-count control allows only 32, 40 or 48; illustrative default 40. Rear tooth-count control allows only 16, 20 or 28; illustrative default 20.
Pedaling frequency ranges from 0 to 2 Hz; illustrative default 1 Hz. Display cadence in rpm using display_scale 60, without changing the SI model.
The crank and front chainring rotate together. An ideal continuous chain engages both sprockets without slip; the sprockets do not mesh directly.
During forward pedaling the rear hub is engaged, so rear sprocket, hub and wheel share the calculated rear rotation frequency.
Fixed illustrative chain pitch is 0.0127 m. Equivalent pitch-circle radii use circumference = tooth count × pitch; these are teaching geometry, not measured bicycle specifications.
Rotation rates are cyclic frequencies in Hz, not angular frequencies. All rotating parts and chain travel use the calculated rates; no elapsed-time input is required.
Steady settings change instantaneously. At zero cadence every modeled moving part stops.
limitations: No coasting, freehub disengagement, shifting transients, torque, pedaling effort, loads, road speed or losses.
Equivalent pitch circles average discrete chain engagement; chordal speed ripple, individual tooth contact and chain articulation are not simulated.
No specific bicycle dimensions, manufacturer specifications or engineering qualification are asserted.
Across all allowed settings: ratio 8/7–3; front frequency 0–2 Hz; rear frequency 0–6 Hz; chain speed 0–1.2192 m/s.
Front equivalent radius is approximately 0.06468–0.09702 m; rear equivalent radius is approximately 0.03234–0.05660 m. All denominators are strictly positive.

definition.title: Bicycle chain drive
definition.description: A simplified cutaway teaching stand connects the crank to a rear wheel through a continuous chain. Illustrative default: 40 front teeth, 20 rear teeth and 60 rpm pedaling produce 120 rpm at the engaged rear wheel.

parts.label: Front tooth count
parts.explanation: Schematic readout overview. Discrete choices 32, 40, 48 only; illustrative default 40.

parts.label: Rear tooth count
parts.explanation: Schematic readout overview. Discrete choices 16, 20, 28 only; illustrative default 20.

parts.label: Pedaling cadence
parts.explanation: Schematic readout overview. Range 0–2 Hz; illustrative default 1 Hz. Display in rpm with scale 60. Also drives crank and front-chainring rotation.

parts.label: Rear-to-front rotation ratio
parts.explanation: Schematic readout overview. Front teeth divided by rear teeth; range 8/7–3.

parts.label: Rear sprocket and wheel cadence
parts.explanation: Schematic readout overview. Shared rear sprocket, engaged hub and wheel frequency: 0–6 Hz. Display rpm using scale 60.

parts.label: Chain travel speed
parts.explanation: Schematic readout overview. Front pitch circumference times pedaling frequency: 0–1.2192 m/s. The same chain speed transfers motion to the rear sprocket.

limits: Only front tooth counts 32, 40, 48 and rear tooth counts 16, 20, 28 are supported. Pedaling cadence is 0–120 rpm; defaults are illustrative.
Rear cadence = pedaling cadence × front teeth / rear teeth. The chain transfers motion without slip; the sprockets do not mesh directly.
Wheel rotation represents only an engaged rear hub during forward pedaling. No coasting, disengagement, shifting transients, torque, effort, loads, road speed or losses are modeled.
Equivalent pitch circles average chain engagement. Individual tooth contacts, articulation and chordal speed ripple are not simulated.
Chain pitch is an illustrative 0.0127 m. Pitch-circle geometry uses 100 scene units per metre; other apparatus dimensions are explicit teaching assumptions, not bicycle specifications.
Ratio range: 8/7–3. Front frequency: 0–2 Hz. Rear frequency: 0–6 Hz. Chain speed: 0–1.2192 m/s. Zero cadence stops all modeled movement.
Front equivalent radius: approximately 0.06468–0.09702 m; rear: 0.03234–0.05660 m. All denominators remain positive.

Sprocket configuration changes instantaneously; chain routing is rebuilt for each selection rather than simulating chain-length adjustment or shifting. Repeated link markings are illustrative, not an asserted physical link count. No tensioner is modeled or implied necessary by this ideal scalar model location choice implies otherwise; this stand uses configuration-specific chain length as a visual

parts.label: Stand base
parts.explanation: This broad base holds the teaching stand steady.

parts.label: Axle supports
parts.explanation: These supports hold the two axles apart so the chain can connect them.

parts.label: Crank bearing housing
parts.explanation: This hollow housing holds the bearings around the crank axle.

parts.label: Inner crank bearing
parts.explanation: Small balls between two rings help the crank axle turn inside its support.

parts.label: Outer crank bearing
parts.explanation: This second bearing supports the other end of the crank axle.

parts.label: Rear bearing housing
parts.explanation: This hollow housing supports the rear axle while it turns.

parts.label: Inner rear bearing
parts.explanation: This bearing guides the rear axle inside its support.

parts.label: Outer rear bearing
parts.explanation: This second rear bearing keeps the axle aligned.

parts.label: Crank rotation
parts.explanation: The crank axle and front chainring turn together at your selected pedaling cadence.

parts.label: Crank axle
parts.explanation: This shaft carries the turning crank through the bearings.

parts.label: Chainring carrier
parts.explanation: This bored flange joins the crank axle to the chainring. A flange is a wide supporting rim.

parts.label: Crank arm
parts.explanation: The crank arm carries your pedaling motion to the axle.

parts.label: Pedal
parts.explanation: The pedal marks where a foot supplies the turning motion. Its separate swiveling motion is not modeled.

parts.label: Front size selection
parts.explanation: Choosing more front teeth makes the chainring larger at the same chain pitch.

parts.label: Front chainring
parts.explanation: The front teeth pull the chain. More front teeth move more chain during each crank turn.

parts.label: Engaged rear rotation
parts.explanation: The rear sprocket, engaged hub and wheel turn together at the calculated rear cadence.

angular_motion.label: Calculated rear cadence — 1× playback, no slowdown

parts.label: Rear shaft
parts.explanation: This simplified stand uses a turning shaft to carry the engaged rear assembly.

parts.label: Engaged rear hub
parts.explanation: The hub is the wheel’s central connector. Here it stays engaged, so the sprocket and wheel turn together.

parts.label: Rear size selection
parts.explanation: Choosing fewer rear teeth makes a smaller sprocket that turns more often for the same chain travel.

parts.label: Rear sprocket
parts.explanation: The moving chain pulls these teeth and turns the engaged rear hub.

parts.label: Wheel spokes
parts.explanation: The spokes connect the hub to the wheel rim.

parts.label: Wheel rim
parts.explanation: The rim joins the spokes and holds the tire.

parts.label: Rear tire
parts.explanation: The tire turns with the rim. This model counts wheel turns, not distance traveled on a road.

parts.label: Continuous chain
parts.explanation: The chain carries motion between the separated sprockets without slipping. Both sprockets share the same chain travel speed.

parts.label: Crank bearing cap
parts.explanation: This removable ring holds the outer bearing in its housing while leaving the axle free to turn.

parts.label: Rear bearing cap
parts.explanation: This removable ring keeps the rear bearing in place without blocking the shaft.

parts.label: Stand fasteners
parts.explanation: These fasteners secure the support feet to the base.

experiments.title: Follow the moving chain
experiments.prompt: Keep both tooth counts fixed. Predict what happens to the chain and wheel when you set pedaling cadence to 90 rpm, then play and compare.
experiments.explanation: The crank turns the chainring, which pulls the chain without slip. The chain turns the rear sprocket; the engaged hub carries that rotation to the wheel. Rear cadence changes proportionally while gear ratio stays fixed. Coasting is not modeled.

experiments.title: Increase front teeth
experiments.prompt: Hold pedaling cadence above zero and keep rear teeth fixed. Predict rear cadence with 48 front teeth, then change the setting and compare.
experiments.explanation: The larger front chainring advances more chain per crank turn. Front teeth divided by rear teeth increases, so rear cadence increases at the same pedaling cadence. Selection changes instantly, without a shifting transient.

experiments.title: Decrease rear teeth
experiments.prompt: Hold pedaling cadence above zero and keep front teeth fixed. Predict rear cadence with 16 rear teeth, then change the setting and compare.
experiments.explanation: A smaller rear sprocket needs less chain travel for each turn. The same chain speed therefore produces more rear turns, shared by the engaged hub and wheel. This predicts rotation only, not effort or road speed.

controls.help: More front teeth increase chain travel per crank turn and rear cadence at fixed pedaling cadence. The default of 40 is illustrative.
Fewer rear teeth increase rear cadence for the same chain speed. The default of 20 is illustrative.
Faster pedaling increases chain speed and rear cadence without changing gear ratio. Zero stops modeled motion. The 60 rpm default is illustrative.

coverage.explanation: Pedaling drives front rotation and calculated chain travel, which drives shared rear sprocket, engaged hub and wheel rotation. Inspectable parts explain their roles; individual tooth contact is not simulated.
At fixed nonzero cadence, increasing front teeth or decreasing rear teeth increases the ratio and rear cadence through front teeth divided by rear teeth.

Cadence scales rear rotation without changing the ratio. Tooth counts change the ratio independently of cadence. Wheel interpretation assumes an engaged rear hub during forward pedaling; coasting, torque, effort, loads, road speed and losses are excluded.

outcomes: Identify how the front chainring, chain, rear sprocket and engaged rear hub transmit rotation to the rear wheel.
Compare rear rotation at the same pedaling cadence when changing front or rear tooth count.
Distinguish the effect of pedaling faster from the effect of changing gear ratio.

generation_quality.scope: Recipe, label, connection and dependency checks only. Dependency paths do not prove numeric change. Overlap, recognizability, physical correctness and child usability require separate evaluation.

visual.scope: Eight fitted views; projected bounds, center-ray occlusion, conservative bounding-box overlaps and estimated two-line label capacity. These heuristics do not replace rendered-image or child usability review.

sampled_quality.scope: Defaults, five points per input plus presets, a midpoint context for apparently inactive controls, all-input endpoints, and lesson experiments. Finite geometry and observed changes only; no proof of scientific accuracy, recognizability or complete state-space coverage.
